scoreNote: Strong-adequate (4.5): a qualified position that concedes comfort can weaken people, then argues that convenience relocates challenges rather than removing them; two developed examples with analysis, controlled prose at about 400 words on a memorable First and Second skeleton.

sentences.text: Every generation seems to worry that comfort is quietly making the next one weak.
Some people argue that the luxuries and conveniences of modern life prevent people from becoming strong and independent individuals.
There is some truth in this worry, but I largely disagree, because convenience does not remove life's challenges so much as change their form.
First, it is fair to admit that too much comfort can sometimes weaken people.
When everything is provided instantly, some people never learn patience or how to struggle through a difficult task.
For example, a student who can find every answer online may never build the discipline needed to solve a hard problem alone.
This shows that convenience, used carelessly, can rob people of the small daily struggles that once built character.
A person who has never had to wait, save, or repair anything may indeed grow impatient and dependent.
Comfort can also make people fragile, so that minor setbacks start to feel like disasters.
To this extent, the worry points to a real danger.
Second, however, convenience does not destroy challenges so much as move them to new areas.
Once machines handle physical labour and basic chores, people are freed to face harder mental and social difficulties instead.
Consider a young entrepreneur who uses modern tools to launch a business, yet still must master risk, failure, and self-discipline to succeed.
Such challenges build independence just as powerfully as hardship once did, only in a different form.
Modern life also gives people more freedom to choose their own path, which itself demands strength and responsibility.
Someone who plans her own career, manages her own money, and shapes her own goals is hardly a weak or passive person.
In this sense, convenience can actually create new chances to grow strong and self-reliant.
In conclusion, comfort can weaken people who let it, but it does not make weakness inevitable.
The challenges that build character have not disappeared; they have simply taken new shapes in work, choice, and responsibility.
Whether convenience makes us weak or strong depends far less on the luxuries themselves than on how we choose to use them.
